analysis.title: US 2026 midterm election update: a final check-in on the polls
key_insights: Generic congressional ballot polling has barely moved in two weeks. RCP shows roughly an 8ppt Democratic advantage, versus a 2.6ppt Republican margin in the cumulative 2024 House vote.

Cook Political Report shifted another 19 House races toward Democrats (18 in the prior update), including six from Toss-up to Lean D, four of them held by Republican incumbents. Cook now sees Democrats gaining 12-22 seats (previously 9-19), or 227-237 of 435.

Democrats need a net gain of three seats for a House majority (218, with the two vacancies assigned to the party that last held them). CACIB puts Democratic House odds at about 90%, in line with betting markets.
Redistricting (gerrymandering) has limited the number of competitive seats, so a 30-40+ seat wave is unlikely. Democrats may end up with only a slender majority.

Senate: Cook moved Minnesota from Likely D to Lean D and South Carolina from Likely R to Lean R. No Toss-up ratings changed. Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and CACIB puts their odds of taking control at about 65%, with Republicans roughly one-in-three to hold.

Senate polling shifts over two weeks were mixed: North Carolina (Cooper +10.6 from +9.0) and Ohio (Brown +3.3 from +3.1) moved toward Democrats, while Iowa flipped to Hinson +0.6 from Turek +0.6 and Texas tightened to Talarico +1.5 from +2.8. Most polled races still give Democrats a slight edge.
Trump's approval is stuck in the high 30% range, with economy approval at 32.5% and inflation approval at 26.8%.

Policy impact: Senate control is not a game changer, since a Trump presidency with a Democratic House likely means legislative gridlock either way. It would matter for judges, other appointments, and oversight and investigations.
Risk flagged: after a comprehensive Republican defeat, Trump could lash out and become more assertive in areas where the executive can act without Congress, such as foreign policy and trade policy.
risk_factors: Polling errors in a few Senate states could change control, since the Senate outlook is close.
Susan Collins in Maine has a history of outperforming her polls.
Trump could escalate trade or foreign policy actions after a comprehensive Republican defeat.
charts_described: Fig 1: the generic congressional ballot (Republican minus Democratic) continues to show a major shift toward Democrats versus the 2024 House vote.
Fig 2: Polymarket odds for the Senate still show Democrats as roughly two-in-three favourites, after a sharp move in their favour earlier in the autumn and more stability in recent weeks.
geopolitical: Possible increased executive assertiveness on foreign policy and trade policy if Republicans suffer a comprehensive midterm defeat

tension_points.bull_case: Democrats are a modest favourite to gain the net four seats needed. Polls in most key states give them a slight edge, and betting markets show roughly two-in-three odds.
tension_points.bear_case: Republicans have roughly a one-in-three chance of narrowly holding the majority. Polls can be off, Maine's Collins has a history of outperforming, and Iowa and Texas have tightened.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A shift in a couple of states over the coming weeks, or a couple of polling errors, could change the outlook.

theme_stances.key_argument: Even the low end of Cook's 12-22 seat range would give Democrats a clear House majority.
theme_stances.evidence: shared by betting markets, that Democrats are a very strong favourite

theme_stances.key_argument: Polling suggests a Democratic advantage in the Senate, but it is a much closer call than the House.
theme_stances.evidence: we still see polling as suggesting a Democratic advantage in 2026
